lead: Every visual display is built for the human eye, a sensor with hard limits. It resolves fine detail only in a tiny central patch, covers roughly 200° of the world with both eyes, and reads depth from a handful of cues. Those numbers tell a designer how many pixels a headset needs, how wide the optics must be, and how much stereo disparity is safe. This chapter covers the eye's structure, its acuity, its field of view and its depth cues, then uses them to explain eye strain in head-mounted displays.
prereq: You need school-level optics (a lens forms an image) and the idea that the retina holds light-sensitive cells; see 3.1 for how the visual channel sits beside audio and haptics.

sections.h3: The eye as an optical instrument

blocks.text: Light passes the cornea, a clear curved surface that supplies about two thirds of the eye's bending power. The iris sets the pupil width, roughly 2 mm in bright light to 8 mm in dim light, trading brightness against sharpness. The lens then fine-tunes focus by changing shape, and that action is accommodation.

Cornea and lens form an image on the retina at the back of the eye. The fovea, a pit about 1.5 mm wide (near 5° of visual angle), sits at its centre and is packed with cones. The optic nerve leaves through the blind spot, which has no photoreceptors.

items: Cones: about 5 million per eye, three colour types, need daylight — photopic vision; densest at the fovea.
Rods: about 100 million per eye, no colour, work in dim light — scotopic vision; almost absent at the fovea, so a faint star shows better slightly off-centre.
Consequence: fine colour detail is seen only in the central few degrees; the rest of the field is coarse and nearly colour-blind.

blocks.text: Photoreceptors do not report absolute brightness; they adapt to the local level over seconds to minutes. That is why a dark room becomes usable after a while, and why a sudden light hurts.

sections.h3: Acuity: the smallest angle the eye can resolve

blocks.text: Acuity is the smallest angle two points can subtend and still be seen as separate. At the fovea in good light it is about 1 arcminute, one sixtieth of a degree, set by the spacing of cones.

blocks.where: θ_min is the minimum resolvable angle; 1 arcminute = 1/60 degree = 2.91 × 10⁻⁴ radians.

blocks.text: A display reaches that limit when each pixel subtends 1 arcminute, which is 60 pixels per degree. The pixel pitch needed at viewing distance D follows.

blocks.where: p is pixel pitch in metres (centre to centre), D is viewing distance in metres, θ_min = 2.91 × 10⁻⁴ rad. At D = 2 m, p ≈ 0.58 mm.

blocks.text: Angle, not size, decides sharpness: a large screen watched from far away and a small screen watched from close look equally sharp if their pixels subtend the same angle. Doubling both size and distance changes nothing.

One eye sees about 160° horizontally and 135° vertically. Two eyes together cover about 200° horizontally with roughly 120° of binocular overlap. Only the central few degrees are sharp, so the eye samples the scene with fast jumps called saccades, about three per second.

sections.h3: Depth cues and why head-mounted displays strain the eyes

blocks.text: Depth perception uses three cue families: binocular (both eyes), monocular (one eye, also present in a photograph) and oculomotor (signals from the eye muscles).

items: Binocular: retinal disparity. An object at distance Z falls on slightly different retinal positions in the two eyes, and the brain converts that shift into depth. The eyes also rotate to meet at the object; that convergence angle is an extra cue. See 3.4 for how displays manufacture disparity.
Monocular: occlusion (near hides far), relative size, linear perspective (parallels converge), shading, texture gradient, and motion parallax (near objects sweep faster as you move).
Oculomotor: convergence (eyes turn in) and accommodation (lens changes shape). Both are reliable only within a few metres.

blocks.text: A head-mounted display focuses its image at a fixed optical distance, for example 2 m, whatever the scene shows. If the scene puts an object at 0.4 m, the eyes converge for 0.4 m while the lens focuses for 2 m. This vergence–accommodation conflict is the main source of eye strain and headache in stereo headsets, and it limits how close rendered objects may appear. Designers keep disparity modest so the eyes never have to diverge.

The visual system also adapts. After long exposure the eyes re-tune, and on removal users may briefly misjudge distance; strong disparities or unusual fields of view leave measurable after-effects. Chapter 3.3 turns these numbers into display choices.

examples.question: A stereo pair is shown on a screen 2 m from a viewer whose eye separation is 6.5 cm. Find the separation between the left and right images on the screen for an object that must appear (a) 1 m away and (b) 4 m away. Use s = e(D/Z − 1), where s is the on-screen separation in cm, e is eye separation, D is the screen distance and Z is the wanted depth in cm.
steps: Write the data in centimetres: e = 6.5 cm, D = 200 cm, and the wanted depths Z = 100 cm and Z = 400 cm.
Positive s means crossed disparity: the left image is placed to the right of the right image, so the lines of sight cross in front of the screen at 1 m.
Negative s means uncrossed disparity: the images sit in the usual order, 3.25 cm apart, and the lines of sight meet behind the screen at 4 m.
examples.answer: The on-screen separations are 6.5 cm crossed for a 1 m object and 3.25 cm uncrossed (−3.25 cm) for a 4 m object.

traps: Accommodation is the lens changing focus; convergence is the eyes turning in. They are different oculomotor cues, and an HMD pulls them apart.
Acuity depends on the angle a pixel subtends, not on screen size. A bigger screen farther away is not sharper.
Crossed disparity places the object nearer than the screen; uncrossed places it farther. Mixing the sign flips the depth.
The fovea holds cones and almost no rods, so night vision is weak exactly where daylight acuity is best.
About 200° is the field of both eyes with the head still; one eye alone gives about 160°.

quiz.a: Cones; the fovea has almost no rods.

quiz.q: State the eye's minimum resolvable angle at the fovea and the matching pixel density.
quiz.a: About 1 arcminute, which is 60 pixels per degree.

quiz.q: Why does acuity fall quickly outside the fovea?
quiz.a: Cone density drops and many rods feed one ganglion cell, so signals are pooled and fine detail blurs.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed-focus head-mounted display cause strain when it draws a near object?
quiz.a: Vergence–accommodation conflict: the eyes converge for the near object while the optics keep the image focused at a fixed distance.

quiz.q: A screen is viewed from 2.5 m. What pixel pitch reaches the acuity limit?
With e = 6.5 cm and D = 200 cm, find s for Z = 2 m and state whether the images are crossed.
quiz.a: s = 6.5 × (200/200 − 1) = 0 cm. The images coincide, there is no disparity, and the object appears on the screen itself.

quiz.q: A photograph of a corridor looks deep. Which depth cues are working and which are missing?
quiz.a: The pictorial monocular cues work: linear perspective, relative size, occlusion, shading, texture gradient. Motion parallax is absent, because a still photograph does not change as the viewer moves. Binocular disparity is absent, because both eyes receive the same image. Convergence and accommodation are present but they lock onto the print's real distance, so they signal a flat surface and fight the depth the picture suggests.

quiz.q: Why do stereo displays keep disparity small instead of using the full screen width?
quiz.a: Large disparity demands strong convergence or divergence, which the eyes cannot follow; fusion breaks, giving double vision and fatigue.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the 60 pixels-per-degree figure drives panel and optic choices, and vergence–accommodation conflict is the target of varifocal and light-field designs. Foveated rendering exploits the sharp-centre, coarse-periphery structure of the retina to cut GPU load. Search next for foveated rendering, varifocal displays, and Panum's fusional area.
